Pipelines & Energy

Keep the line covered, supported and in service.

Creeks, rivers and drainage areas can move long after a pipeline is installed. When cover is lost or banks retreat, pipelines can be exposed to vehicles, vandalism and, in some cases, loads they were never designed to withstand.

What we see in pipelines & energy.

What you're seeingWhat's driving itHow we solve it
What you're seeing

The pipeline is exposed at a water crossing.

Cover has washed out and the pipeline is visible in the bed or banks of a water crossing.

What's driving it

Bed degradation and scour at the crossing, often set off by changes upstream or downstream that lower the channel.

How we solve it

We investigate the crossing and trace the cause, then engineer and permit protection that restores cover and holds the bed in place.

What you're seeing

A span needs support.

The designed span in a ravine has eroded because the ground beneath it has washed away and the span needs mechanical support.

What's driving it

An engineered crossing that calls for support, or flow that has removed material beneath the line faster than the channel can rebuild it.

How we solve it

We engineer and install support under the span and, where erosion created the condition, stabilize the surrounding site.

What you're seeing

The bank is eroding due to lateral migration.

The outside bend is eroding and endangering the nearby pipeline.

What's driving it

High-velocity flow concentrated against the bank as the channel migrates.

How we solve it

We model how the river is behaving and redirect the flow away from the bank, armoring it where the river leaves no room to recover.

What you're seeing

A knickpoint is moving toward the pipeline.

A step or drop in the channel bed is working its way upstream toward the pipeline crossing.

What's driving it

A lowered channel downstream. Every flow event pushes the drop further upstream.

How we solve it

We engineer grade control that stops the knickpoint where it is and stabilizes the channel through the crossing.

In the field

Meandering creeks see changing water levels and flow rates, and they can expose a pipeline quickly. We rebuilt this bank as a stepped wall over the line.

Over time, erosion can leave a pipeline spanning a ravine it was never meant to cross. That calls for prompt work: support beneath the pipeline and armoring around it.

A headcut was cutting its way upstream through open ground, taking more land with every storm. We installed stepped grade control to stop the knickpoint and step the water down safely to the channel below.

Flow through this road crossing had cut the bank beside it back toward the road. We rebuilt the bank and armored it where the flow leaves the crossing.

Below a roadway, runoff cut this drainage channel deep into red clay and exposed the line running through it. We rebuilt it as a lined channel, from the road culvert down, that holds its grade.

Debris and high flows scoured this creek crossing until the line beneath it was exposed. We restored the cover and rebuilt the crossing over new culverts.

The river was taking this bank, and the farmland above it, with every high water event. Five years after the work, the bank is rebuilt and green.

Runoff at this processing plant had carved the drainage under the pipe racks into open ditches. We lined the channel to protect the ground the supports stand on and mitigate sediment flow.

When a river starts cutting toward a transmission line, the structures beside it are next. We armored the banks and channels to protect the utility infrastructure.
